summary: This wiki page is a broad overview of modern history from the 1800s through the mid-20th century, with sections on the Franco-Prussian War, the Mughal and Maratha empires, Napoleon, British India and the Victorian era, the Holocaust, the Russian Revolution and Civil War, the League of Nations crises, and the Cold War. Each section covers a different region or conflict, and the note presents them as separate narratives rather than one continuous chronology. The sections are drawn from the note's text only.
one_line: A broad overview of modern world history, covering 19th- and 20th-century wars, empires, revolutions, and the Cold War across several regions.
key_facts: The Franco-Prussian War was fought between France and Prussia, with Prussia backed by the North German Confederation and the South German states of Baden, Württemberg and Bavaria.
The Prussian and German victory in the Franco-Prussian War brought about the final unification of Germany under King Wilhelm I of Prussia.
The Franco-Prussian War marked the downfall of Napoleon III and the end of the Second French Empire, which was replaced by the Third Republic.
As part of the Franco-Prussian settlement, Prussia took almost all of the territory of Alsace-Lorraine, which it retained until the end of World War I.
The classic period of the Mughal Empire ended with the death and defeat of Emperor Aurangzeb in 1707 by the rising Hindu Maratha Empire, although the dynasty continued for another 150 years.
In 1761 the Maratha army lost the Third Battle of Panipat, which halted imperial expansion, and the Maratha empire was then divided into a confederacy of Maratha states.
In the 1970s the regimes of the Southern Cone collaborated in Operation Condor, killing many leftist dissidents, and by the early 1990s all countries had restored their democracies.
Napoleon Bonaparte was born on Corsica as the French invaded and died suspiciously on the tiny British island of St. Helena.
The Cold War included international crises such as the Berlin Blockade (1948–1949), the Korean War (1950–1953), the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) and the Soviet war in Afghanistan (1979–1989).
The Maratha states lost to the British East India Company in 1818 with the Third Anglo-Maratha War.
In 1819 Stamford Raffles established Singapore as a key trading post for Britain in its rivalry with the Dutch.
Queen Victoria's reign, which defines the Victorian era of the United Kingdom, ran from June 1837 to January 1901.
The Holocaust was the deliberate and systematic murder of millions of Jews and other unwanted groups during World War II by the Nazi regime in Germany.
The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed between Russia and the Central Powers in 1917, conceded huge portions of the former Russian Empire to Imperial Germany and the Ottoman Empire.
In October 1917 the Red Guard, directed by the Bolshevik Party, seized Saint Petersburg (then Petrograd) and began an armed takeover of cities and villages across the former Russian Empire.
The League of Nations failed to stop Italy's 1935/36 invasion of Abyssinia despite economic sanctions, and Hitler then remilitarized the Rhineland in violation of the Treaty of Versailles.
